result.question: I suspect our past work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN have been coded inconsistently, which makes our fault history useless for trending. Pull all work orders on Transformer 1, open and closed, and show me each one's number, description, status and failure code. Then read our failure code catalog and map each code to the closest transformer fault class or failure mode: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core/winding thermal, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. Flag every work order whose code doesn't match its description, and every one that has no code at all, and suggest the correct code for each. Also run a fault classification on the latest oil sample and tell me whether any open work order is coded for a different fault than the gases currently indicate. Only propose recodes, and don't change anything yourself unless the work order is still open and the description clearly names the fault. In that case, update its failure code and list what you changed. If the catalog has no code that fits a fault class, say so and recommend a new code rather than forcing a poor match.
result.answer:
I made no changes. Transformer 1 has only two work orders, both still open. One is coded correctly. The other has no code because the catalog has nothing that fits it.

**Work orders on Transformer 1 (MAIN)**
There are no closed work orders on this asset. So there is no past fault history to trend yet.

| WO | Description | Status | Failure code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000052 | Oil sample retest (DGA) and insulation check – Transformer 1 thermal fault | WAPPR (open) | FC006 |
| 1000051 | OLTC inspection – on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking) | WAPPR (open) | none |

**Catalog codes mapped to transformer fault classes**
The catalog has 10 general equipment codes. Only one is a reasonable match for a transformer fault class.

| Code | Catalog description | Closest fault class | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| FC006 | overheating or high temperature reading | Oil overheating / core-winding thermal | Good, but one code covers both classes |
| FC004 | fluid leak observed | Moisture ingress (a leak is a way in for moisture) | Poor: it records the symptom, not the fault |
| FC003 | abnormal noise | Maybe arcing or core looseness | Poor: don't use it |
| FC001, FC002, FC005, FC007–FC010 | start/stop, vibration, indicator, gauge, structural, loose part | None | None |

These fault classes have no suitable code: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing and oil dielectric degradation. Oil overheating and core/winding thermal can't be told apart because both fall under FC006.

**Recommended new codes** (names are suggestions):
- TX-PD: partial discharge
- TX-D1: low-energy arcing/sparking
- TX-D2: high-energy arcing
- TX-T-OIL: oil overheating (under 300 °C)
- TX-T-HOT: core/winding thermal (300–700 °C and above)
- TX-OLTC: tap changer contact wear/coking
- TX-H2O: moisture ingress
- TX-PAPER: cellulose ageing
- TX-OILDIEL: oil dielectric degradation

**Work orders to flag**
- **1000052:** FC006 matches the thermal-fault description. No recode needed. Once a TX-T-HOT code exists, it would be the more specific choice.
- **1000051:** It has no code. The description clearly names tap changer wear, but no catalog code fits. FC006 or FC010 would be a forced, poor match, so I left it blank. Proposed code: the new TX-OLTC.

**Fault classification on the latest oil sample (2024-01-19)**
The DGA interpretation tool failed twice ("LLM unavailable"), so I worked out the IEC 60599 Rogers ratios by hand.
- **Readings:** H₂ 2850, CH₄ 7400, C₂H₂ 7, C₂H₄ 16650, C₂H₆ 5470, CO 32, CO₂ 1340 (all ppm)
- **Ratios:**
  - C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = 0.0004 (code 0)
  - CH₄/H₂ = 2.60 (code 2)
  - C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = 3.04 (code 2, only just above 3)
- **Result:** The code pattern 0-2-2 points to a thermal fault above 700 °C (T3), which is core/winding thermal. It sits right on the boundary with the 300–700 °C band (T2).
- **Cross-check:** On the Duval triangle, C₂H₄ is 69% and C₂H₂ is 0.03%, which is also T3. Acetylene is negligible, so there's no sign of arcing.
- **Paper insulation:** CO₂/CO is about 42 and CO is low, so the paper insulation doesn't appear to be involved.

**Do the open work orders match the gases?**
- **1000052 (FC006, thermal):** Consistent with the gases.
- **1000051:** It is uncoded, but the fault it describes (tap changer wear) doesn't match what the main-tank gases show, which is a core/winding hot spot. Tap changer coking would only show up this way if the tap changer compartment leaks into the main tank. Consider checking that tap changer oil sample before treating this as a tap changer problem.
- It is also set to priority 1, higher than 1000052 at priority 3. Its target start date (2024-01-19) is out of date.

**Changes made:** None. 1000052 is already coded correctly. 1000051 needs a new tap changer code added to the catalog before it can be coded.

details.suggestions: The agent covered the core requirements: listed all Transformer 1 work orders with number/description/status/failure code, read the failure code catalog, mapped codes to transformer fault classes, flagged the uncoded work order, identified catalog gaps with recommended new codes, and correctly refrained from updates (FC006 already fits 1000052; no catalog code fits 1000051). When fmsr.interpret_dga failed twice with 'LLM unavailable', it transparently fell back to manual Rogers/IEC ratio and Duval computations, which are arithmetically correct (CH4/H2=2.60, C2H4/C2H6=3.04, C2H2/C2H4≈0.0004 → T2/T3 boundary thermal fault, no arcing). However, the expected sequence was not fully followed: it never called wo.get_workorder for per-order detail nor fmsr.get_failure_modes to cross-check the fault-class mapping against the FMSR knowledge base, and the list_workorders output is recorded as null in the trace, so the work-order details could not be independently verified from the log (they appear plausible and internally consistent, so this is treated as a logging artifact rather than fabrication). Recommend calling fmsr.get_failure_modes for the mapping cross-check, and noting explicitly that the DGA classification is a manual fallback with the IEC 60599 vs Rogers boundary caveat (3.04 is T2 under IEC 60599's >4 threshold for T3, T3 under Rogers).
